strengths: The paper targets an important challenge in LLM fine-tuning: moving beyond rote imitation in supervised fine-tuning (SFT) by incorporating explanatory critique signals into the distillation process.
The empirical evaluation covers a broad suite of reasoning and general NLP benchmarks (MATH500, Minerva-Math, GSM8K, OlympiadBench, AMC23, TheoremQA, GPQA, MMLU-Pro, IFEval, MUSR, BBH, TruthfulQA).
The paper is generally well-structured and easy to read, with clear illustrative diagrams comparing SFT, CFT, and CGD.
weaknesses: Critical ambiguity and potential methodological flaw regarding inference time: CGD trains the student model on the objective $\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{x, y', c, \hat{y}} [-\log S_\theta(\hat{y} \mid x, y', c)]$ (Eq. 1, Figure 1, Algorithm 1). In Section 4.4 and Figure 5, the paper explicitly differentiates between 'CGD' (which takes critique $c$ in the input) and 'CGD without critique'. However, the manuscript never explains where $y'$ and $c$ come from at test time on benchmark datasets. If teacher critiques $c$ from LLaMA3.3-70B are supplied at test time, the evaluation is not evaluating an autonomous 8B student model, and directly contradicts the explicit claims that CGD incurs 'no additional inference-time cost' (Section 5) and 'significantly lower inference overhead' (Section 1). If teacher critiques are not provided at test time, the paper fails to describe how the student generates answers given only prompt $x$ despite being trained on $(x, y', c)$.

Lemma 1 and its proof in Section 3.1 contain fatal mathematical errors: (1) The lemma defines $KL(P(X) \parallel Q(Y|Z))$, which is mathematically undefined as $P(X)$ and $Q(Y|Z)$ are probability distributions over different random variables ($X$ vs. $Y$). (2) In Equations (3) and (4), the summation is over $x$, but $Q(y|z)$ contains un-indexed free variables $y$ and $z$. (3) The application of Jensen's inequality is inverted. By Jensen's inequality for the convex function $-\log(\cdot)$, $-\log \sum_c Q(y|z,c) Pr(c|z) \le -\sum_c Pr(c|z) \log Q(y|z,c)$. Because of the negative sign in the expansion of KL divergence, Eq. (3) is less than or equal to Eq. (4), which proves the exact opposite of Eq. (6). The inequality was simply flipped to fit the desired claim.

The Bayesian interpretation in Section 3.2 (Eq. 10) is mathematically heuristic and disconnected from the implementation: Eq. (10) ad-hoc combines the student posterior $S_\theta$, the teacher likelihood $T_\phi$, and the initial student prior $S_{init}$ into Bayes' theorem as if they were components of a single coherent generative model. Furthermore, Algorithm 1 does not optimize a posterior update or likelihood-weighted objective; it performs standard maximum likelihood estimation on teacher-generated targets $\hat{y}$.

Missing crucial experimental details: The paper omits the exact inference prompt templates, decoding hyperparameters (temperature, top-p, max tokens), and an explicit description of the test-time evaluation protocol, hindering reproducibility.

strengths: The core intuition—leveraging teacher-generated critiques to supervise answer refinement rather than training the model solely to critique or mimic raw answers—addresses an important challenge in LLM fine-tuning.

The empirical evaluation is broad, covering both mathematical reasoning benchmarks (MATH500, Minerva-Math, GSM8K, OlympiadBench, AMC23) and broader reasoning/instruction-following tasks (MMLU-Pro, GPQA, IFEval, BBH).
The analysis of Critique Fine-Tuning (CFT) suffering from format drift and performance collapse on general benchmarks (e.g., IFEval) is insightful.
weaknesses: Severe ambiguity and potential invalidity in the test-time inference procedure: Throughout Sections 1, 3, Algorithm 1, and Figure 1/2, CGD is defined as training the student to predict the refined response given the prompt, the student's initial response, and the critique: $S_\theta(\hat{y} | x, y', c)$. However, the paper never specifies how inference is conducted at test time. If the teacher model ($70\text{B}$) is queried at test time to generate critiques $c$, the comparison to standard fine-tuned $8\text{B}$ models is fundamentally invalid and contradicts claims of 'significantly lower inference overhead' and having no 'additional inference-time cost'. If the teacher is not used at test time, it is unexplained how $c$ and $y'$ are obtained or how a student trained on $(x, y', c)$ can be prompted with $x$ alone without severe distribution shift.

Fundamental mathematical errors in the theoretical analysis (Lemma 1 and Section 3.1): In Lemma 1, the proof applies Jensen's inequality to $-\log \sum_c Q(y|z, c) \Pr(c|z) \le -\sum_c \Pr(c|z) \log Q(y|z, c)$. However, because this term is subtracted in the KL divergence expansion, this inequality directly implies that $\text{KL}(R(X) \parallel Q(Y|Z)) \le \text{KL}(R(X) \parallel Q(Y|Z, C))$, the exact opposite of the claimed inequality in Eq. (2) and Eq. (9). Furthermore, the notation conflates random variables ($X, Y, Z, C$) and marginals/conditionals ($R(x)$ vs $Q(y|z)$) across different supports without well-defined probability spaces.

Inconsistency in the Bayesian formulation: Eq. (10) formulates the teacher likelihood as $T_\phi(c | x, y', \hat{y})$, where critique $c$ is conditioned on the refined response $\hat{y}$. Yet in Algorithm 1 (lines 6–7), $c$ is generated conditionally on $(x, y')$ before $\hat{y}$, and $\hat{y}$ is sampled conditioned on $(x, y', c)$. The theoretical framing does not correspond to the actual algorithmic data generation process.

Lack of essential baseline controls: If CGD operates at test time via a multi-step pipeline (generating an initial answer, generating a critique, and refining), it must be benchmarked against standard inference-time self-refinement / multi-pass prompting baselines (e.g., Self-Refine, Reflexion) under matched computational budgets.

strengths: Addressing the limitation of imitation learning in SFT by incorporating explanatory critique and refinement during training is an important and practically relevant research direction.

The experimental evaluation considers a wide range of benchmarks spanning mathematical reasoning (MATH500, AMC23, OlympiadBench, GSM8K), general reasoning (TheoremQA, GPQA, MMLU-Pro), and instruction following (IFEval, BBH).
The analysis regarding format drift in Critique Fine-Tuning (CFT) and its detrimental impact on instruction following (e.g., on IFEval) offers an interesting empirical observation.
weaknesses: Critical lack of clarity and potential evaluation invalidity regarding test-time inference: The paper defines CGD training (Eq. 1, Algorithm 1, Figure 1, Figure 2) as training the student model on the input tuple (x, y', c) to predict the refined answer \hat{y}, where y' is an initial response and c is the teacher's critique. However, the manuscript never specifies how evaluation is performed at test time on benchmarks like MATH500, AMC23, or MMLU-Pro. If the test-time input includes the teacher critique c, the evaluation is fundamentally flawed because teacher critiques directly reveal errors and solution steps (as seen in Figure 1 and Appendix A.1), giving an unfair advantage over baselines and rendering the claim of 'no extra inference cost' false. If c is not provided at test time, there is an unaddressed, severe train-test input distribution mismatch that contradicts the paper's formulation and figures. In either case, the core experimental setup is either invalid or completely unrepeatable.

Mathematical error in Lemma 1: The proof of Lemma 1 relies on Jensen's inequality in Eq. (5): -\log \sum_c Q(y|z, c) Pr(c|z) \le -\sum_c Pr(c|z) \log Q(y|z, c). In Eq. (3) and (4), this term is preceded by a negative sign in the expansion of the KL divergence. Consequently, substituting the inequality yields KL(R(X) || Q(Y|Z)) \le KL(R(X) || Q(Y|Z, C)), which is the exact opposite of the claimed inequality in Eq. (2) and Eq. (6). The inequality was inverted to support the authors' narrative.

Ill-posed theoretical formulation: In Lemma 1, the authors write KL(P(X) || Q(Y|Z)), comparing a marginal distribution over X with a conditional distribution over Y given Z, where y and z appear as unbound free variables in the summation. Furthermore, concluding in Eq. (9) that this KL relationship implies the model 'starts optimizing from a better point' is theoretically meaningless, as optimization begins at parameter initialization \theta_{init}, not from a KL divergence bound.

Unsubstantiated Bayesian interpretation: Section 3.2 asserts in Eq. (10) that S_\theta(\hat{y} | x, y', c) factorizes as a student prior S_{init} multiplied by a teacher likelihood T_\phi(c | x, y', \hat{y}). Minimizing standard cross-entropy loss on teacher-generated outputs \hat{y} (Eq. 1) does not enforce or implement this posterior factorization, making the Bayesian claims purely hand-waving.

Suspicious baseline degradation: Standard SFT severely underperforms the base model Llama-3.1-8B Instruct (e.g., MATH500 drops from 50.6% to 41.2%, Minerva-Math from 33.5% to 24.6%, and Group 1 average drops from 41.3% to 35.5%). Such massive degradation indicates poor hyperparameter tuning or flawed training pipelines for the baselines, undermining the credibility of the reported empirical gains.

strengths: The core motivation is clear: supervised fine-tuning often encourages rote imitation of final answers rather than deliberate reasoning, while multi-pass critique/refinement methods incur significant inference latency.

The empirical evaluation is extensive across diverse benchmarks, including mathematical reasoning (MATH-500, AMC23, OlympiadBench, Minerva-Math), general reasoning (TheoremQA, GPQA, MMLU-Pro), and instruction following (IFEval, BBH).
The paper provides an extensive set of appendices exploring student/teacher model variations, learning rate sensitivity, data mixture ratios, and training loss stability.
weaknesses: Fundamental contradiction and lack of clarity between the inference protocol and mechanistic analyses: The paper repeatedly emphasizes as a primary contribution that at inference time, CGD requires only the original prompt $x$ and generates the refined answer in a single pass without needing initial answers or critiques (Abstract, Figure 1, Section 1, Figure 3, Section 3.2). However, the training objective in Eq. (1) strictly trains the student on $\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}[-\log S_\theta(\hat{y} \mid x, y', c)]$. There is zero technical explanation of how an autoregressive model trained exclusively to generate $\hat{y}$ given the full context $(x, y', c)$ is prompted or adapted at inference time when given only $x$. More critically, all diagnostic and mechanistic analyses in Appendix C (entropy in C.1/C.2, gradient norm in Table 10, attention analysis in C.3, and counterfactual evaluation in C.4) explicitly feed the full context $(x, y', c)$ into the model. In Section C.3, the authors argue that CGD's success is driven by the model attending heavily to the critique (e.g., 48.1% of attention in Layer 31) during initial generation phases. If the model depends on the critique prefix to structure its reasoning, how can it function when the critique is absent at inference time? This discrepancy severely undermines the soundness of the core claims.

Misleading compute efficiency comparison against RL baselines: The comparison to SimpleRL-Zero (Section 4.2.1 and Abstract) claims that CGD approaches or exceeds RL performance while requiring '60x less compute' based solely on the 8 A100 GPU-hours of student fine-tuning. This comparison completely disregards the enormous computational cost of generating 100,000 student initial rollouts, 100,000 teacher critiques, and 100,000 teacher refined answers using LLaMA-3.3-70B-Instruct. SimpleRL-Zero is a zero-teacher RL method; comparing distillation from a 70B teacher against zero-teacher RL while omitting the teacher generation cost is methodologically unfair.

Unconvincing and degrading SFT baselines: In Table 1, standard SFT shows substantial degradation relative to the base LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct model (e.g., MATH-500 drops from 50.6% to 41.2%, Minerva-Math drops from 33.5% to 24.6%, and OlympiadBench drops from 14.5% to 10.8%). While fine-tuning on noisy web data can cause alignment tax, such a severe degradation suggests suboptimal baseline tuning or format mismatch rather than intrinsic SFT limits, weakening the empirical claims.

Superficial mathematical framing: The Bayesian interpretation presented in Section 3.2 and Appendix C.5 ($S_\theta(\hat{y} \mid x, y', c) \propto T_\phi(c \mid x, y', \hat{y}) \times S_{\text{init}}(\hat{y} \mid x, y')$) is purely post-hoc notation. The training procedure in Algorithm 1 is standard cross-entropy teacher distillation on teacher-generated outputs; framing it as Bayesian posterior update via KL divergence minimization adds no algorithmic or theoretical substance.

strengths: Compelling high-level motivation: the paper targets an important dilemma in LLM reasoning—how to leverage rich critique and self-correction signals during training without incurring the inference latency of multi-turn prompting or the format drift associated with critique-generation methods like CFT.

Extensive evaluation across diverse benchmarks: the empirical study evaluates multiple reasoning benchmarks (MATH-500, Minerva-Math, GSM8K, OlympiadBench, AMC23, TheoremQA, GPQA, MMLU-Pro) as well as broader instruction-following and safety benchmarks (IFEval, BBH, TruthfulQA, MUSR).

Broad validation across model families and scales: experiments include both LLaMA-3.1-8B and S1.1-3B students, with cross-architecture tests on Mixtral-8x7B and OLMo-2-7B, as well as ablations with different teacher models (LLaMA-3.3-70B and S1.1-32B).

Insightful ablation on training critique composition: the experiment analyzing the ratio of correct to incorrect initial student answers (Appendix B.1.4, Figure 5) provides an interesting empirical takeaway showing that a balanced 50/50 mixture yields the strongest results.
weaknesses: Severe ambiguity and apparent contradiction between the training objective and the inference protocol: The training loss (Eq. 1 and Algorithm 1) explicitly optimizes $S_\theta(\hat{y} \mid x, y', c)$ where the student conditions on the prompt $x$, initial response $y'$, and critique $c$. Yet, the abstract, Section 1, and Figure 3 repeatedly claim that at test time, the model is fed only the prompt $x$ and directly predicts $\hat{y}$ in a single pass. If the model was trained exclusively conditioned on $(x, y', c)$, testing on $x$ alone constitutes a drastic input format and distribution shift. The paper never explains what prompt template is fed at test time, whether prefix/conditioning dropout was used during training, or how the model bridges this gap. If test-time prompting is $x \to \hat{y}$, why would this outperform Distilled SFT (which is directly trained on $x \to \hat{y}$)? This critical gap undermines the technical soundness of the core contribution.

Diagnostic analyses evaluate a mismatched setup: The mechanistic interpretability and attention analyses (Figures 9–11), as well as the diagnostic entropy and gradient norm calculations (Tables 9–10), evaluate the model when explicitly fed the full $(x, y', c)$ context. Since the primary claim of the paper is that CGD succeeds at test time given only the prompt $x$ without critiques, analyzing attention directed toward the critique during generation does not explain how the model functions when the critique is entirely absent at inference.

Misleading compute comparison with RL (Section 4.2.1, Table 3): The claim that CGD achieves comparable performance to SimpleRL-Zero while requiring '60x less compute' is fundamentally misleading. SimpleRL-Zero trains from scratch via pure reinforcement learning without teacher supervision. In contrast, CGD relies on 100K synthetic training triplets generated by a 70B parameter teacher model (requiring initial student generation, teacher critique generation, and teacher refinement generation). Factoring in the inference compute needed to produce 200,000 passes through a 70B model completely changes the compute ledger.

Superficial and mathematically loose 'Bayesian interpretation': Section 3.2 and Appendix C.5 frame CGD as Bayesian posterior inference via Eq. 2, but this formulation is purely cosmetic and technically unsound. If the critique $c$ acts as evidence updating the prior $P(y \mid x)$ into the posterior $P(y \mid x, c)$, it is mathematically impossible for the model at inference time to sample from this critique-informed posterior if the evidence $c$ is not provided.

Unclear training throughput reporting: Section 4.1.2 states that all fine-tuning runs on 100k examples with maximum sequence length 8192 were trained on 16 Nvidia A100 GPUs for 30 minutes (8 GPU-hours total). This implies processing ~3.5 samples per GPU per second for an 8B model under ZeRO-3, which seems extraordinarily fast unless the vast majority of sequences were very short. More specific details on mean sequence lengths and effective token throughput are necessary to assess reproducibility.

strengths: The paper explores an important problem: overcoming the limitations of standard supervised fine-tuning and critique fine-tuning (CFT) by incorporating critique-guided corrections into model training.

Extensive empirical evaluations are conducted across multiple reasoning and general benchmarks (MATH-500, AMC23, OlympiadBench, MMLU-Pro, IFEval) across diverse model families (LLaMA, s1.1/Qwen, Mixtral, OLMo).
The paper includes thoughtful ablations examining different teacher models, learning rates, and the mixture ratio of correct versus incorrect student answers in training data.
weaknesses: Fundamental contradiction between the training formulation and the claimed inference procedure: Equation 1 and Algorithm 1 define the training objective as predicting the refined response conditioned on the full triplet of prompt, initial student response, and teacher critique: S_theta(y_hat | x, y', c). However, the paper repeatedly claims (Abstract, Section 1, Section 3.1, Figure 3) that at inference time, CGD takes only the prompt x and directly outputs y_hat in a single pass. For standard autoregressive decoder-only models, conditioning on [x, y', c] during training means that providing only [x] at test time constitutes an extreme input format mismatch; the model would naturally attempt to generate y' rather than jump to y_hat. The manuscript never explains or formalizes how this discrepancy is resolved.

Contradiction between claimed critique-free inference and the diagnostic experiments: While the main text claims the student model does not require the critique at inference time, the mechanistic experiments in Appendix C directly contradict this. Specifically, Section C.1, C.3 (Figures 9–11), and Section C.4 (Table 11) explicitly supply the initial answer and the critique in the prompt during evaluation. Furthermore, the paper claims that attention to critique tokens (48.1% in Layer 31) proves the model 'internalizes the critique's guidance,' but this is simply standard in-context attention to tokens physically present in the prompt context, not evidence of weight internalization for critique-free generation.

Unfair compute comparison to RL-Zero: Section 4.2.1 compares CGD to SimpleRL-Zero and claims an order-of-magnitude reduction in compute (60x less). This comparison is fundamentally flawed: SimpleRL-Zero performs reinforcement learning from scratch without teacher supervision, whereas CGD relies on 100k high-quality demonstrations synthesized by a 70B teacher model (LLaMA-3.3-70B-Instruct). Omitting the pretraining and inference costs of generating 100k critiques and refined answers from a 70B teacher makes the efficiency claims misleading.

Underperforming SFT baseline: In Table 1, standard SFT substantially degrades the base model's performance on math tasks (e.g., LLaMA-3.1-8B Instruct drops from 50.6% to 41.2% on MATH500, and from 33.5% to 24.6% on Minerva-Math). Such severe degradation indicates poor hyperparameter tuning or dataset quality issues for the SFT baseline, making the relative gains over SFT less convincing.

Superficial Bayesian framing: The probabilistic framing in Section 3.2 and Appendix C.5 merely asserts a proportionality relationship (Equation 2) without executing any genuine Bayesian learning, variational bound, or posterior sampling mechanism. Standard cross-entropy fine-tuning on teacher demonstrations is not Bayesian inference, and the framing adds conceptual confusion rather than technical rigor.

Presentation and typography flaws: Figure 7 contains broken LaTeX font encodings ('10¡6', '2 £ 10¡6', '3 £ 10¡64 £ 10¡6'), Figure 4 has overlapping text labels, and several bibliographic entries are malformed (e.g., 'and et al..' in Lin et al., 2024).
